analysis.one_liner: Bars new retirement contributions by people with over $10 million already saved and forces faster withdrawals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says that once someone has more than $10 million across their retirement accounts, and their income is above roughly $400,000–$450,000 a year, they can no longer put new money into retirement accounts, which get special tax treatment. Starting in 2034, people with balances above $10 million would also have to pull out half of whatever they have over that cap each year — with Roth accounts drained first — and those forced withdrawals would be subject to 37 percent federal withholding. Retirement accounts are the biggest legal tax shelter available, and a small number of households have accumulated eight- and nine-figure balances inside them; this bill would end the unlimited version of that shelter.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: the tax subsidy for retirement saving is currently unlimited for the wealthiest savers, so people with $10 million-plus balances can shelter enormous sums from tax for decades. Closing that open-ended shelter makes the tax system somewhat fairer and preserves the accounts' tax advantages for the savers they were designed for. Savers affected by the bill also gain some flexibility — the bill lets them withdraw the excess amounts without the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle-income retirement savers and general taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Once a taxpayer has more than $10 million in vested retirement balances, the bill prohibits any further tax-favored contributions to retirement plans by or on their behalf.
The contribution ban applies to people whose income was above $225,000 (single), $400,000 (most others), or $450,000 (married filing jointly) in the prior year.

Starting in 2034, people with balances over $10 million must distribute at least half of the amount above $10 million each year, with Roth IRA and designated Roth account balances drawn down first; these accelerated distributions are exempt from the 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty.

Distributions made to satisfy the accelerated requirement are treated as nonperiodic distributions subject to 37 percent withholding, and no election can reduce that withholding, except for qualified Roth distributions.
The income thresholds and the $10 million balance cap are indexed to inflation after 2027.

analysis.who_pays: The direct cost falls on households with retirement balances above $10 million and high incomes: they lose the ability to keep adding tax-deferred money, and starting in 2034 they must draw down and pay tax on half of their excess balance each year. Plan administrators, employers, and financial firms would bear new compliance duties — plans must allow these mandatory withdrawals on demand, and withholding agents must apply the 37 percent rate.

drawbacks.text: The Roth-first drawdown rule breaks the long-standing promise that Roth accounts are never taxed again: money someone already paid tax on and moved into a Roth would be forced out first, which critics would call a retroactive change to settled rules.
A 37 percent withholding rate on the forced distributions, with no election to lower it, creates a large up-front cash-flow hit that affected taxpayers would only reconcile at filing time.

The compliance load is real: qualified plans, 403(b) custodial and annuity contracts, and governmental 457 plans must all add on-demand distribution rights, and administrators must value and aggregate balances across every plan a person holds — the bill itself needed special rules for ESOPs and non-readily-tradable employer stock to avoid trapping people.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the revenue comes from a very small number of households, so the bill is more about tax fairness at the top than about funding anything specific — the bill text directs the revenue to no new program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is well-targeted at a genuine loophole — unlimited tax-sheltered accumulation for the very wealthy — and it carefully exempts rollovers, inheritances, and divorce transfers so people are not penalized for events they didn't choose. The Roth-first sequencing and 37 percent withholding are blunt and would be the fair points of dispute for the affected households. On balance, the design is more careful than typical tax provisions aimed at the wealthy, though its value to ordinary people depends entirely on whether the revenue and fairness principle are actually pursued.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on July 21, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
As of the latest action record, the Finance Committee has taken no further action on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: households with mega retirement balances keep today's unlimited shelter, and the bill's prospects rest entirely on whether the Finance Committee acts before the Congress ends.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee, of which he has been a senior member and former ranking member.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and there are no cosponsors, so the partisan shape is unknown; the only recorded action is a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: These households lose the ability to keep piling money into tax-sheltered accounts and, from 2034, must draw down and pay tax on half of anything above $10 million each year. Their interest in keeping the current rules runs against the general taxpayer's interest in a tax system where the largest balances are not permanently sheltered.

Firms managing mega-balance accounts would lose some of the incentive to funnel unlimited deferrals into their products, but the bill creates new administrative work (on-demand distribution rights, cross-plan valuation, 37 percent withholding) that firms would handle for fees.

Plans must amend to allow these withdrawals on request and aggregate balances for compliance, adding cost — but the burden falls on servicing high-income mega-accounts, not on ordinary participants, who are untouched by the thresholds.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors, introduced in late July of an election-year Congress and sitting in the Finance Committee, is unlikely to move: most bills at this stage never get a hearing. It would realistically advance only if attached to a broader tax package, as similar retirement-balance limits have been in past Democratic tax proposals.
